content.intro: You'll learn to introduce yourself, say where you're from, and ask someone else the same in an informal setting. The main trap: Paraguay uses 'vos' instead of 'tú', so the question forms you may have learned elsewhere (¿cómo te llamas?, ¿de dónde eres?) sound foreign here — you need ¿cómo te llamás? and ¿de dónde sos?.

vocab.note: Voseo subject + verb, replaces 'tú eres' entirely in Paraguay.
Voseo form; not ¿cómo te llamas?
Voseo form of ser.
Adjust for your own gender.
Voseo; a common follow-up after names.
Interchangeable with encantado/a, slightly more common casually.

exercises.prompt: You've just sat down next to someone at a bus stop. Greet them and introduce yourself with your name.
The person asks where you're from. Answer them, then ask them the same question using voseo.
Ask a new acquaintance for their name and what they do for work, both using voseo forms.
You're at a friend's family asado and someone new walks up to the group. Introduce yourself to them, ask their name, where they're from, and what they do — keep it flowing as one short conversation.

content.intro: This is the single most useful lesson in A1: phrases to keep a conversation going when you mishear or don't know a word, instead of freezing or switching to English. The trap: 'repetir' and 'repetime' need the voseo command form, so it's ¿me repetís? and repetime, not the tú forms you may expect.

vocab.gloss: can you repeat that for me, please?
vocab.note: Voseo; casual but polite with 'por favor'.
Voseo command of deletrear; used constantly in Paraguay for names over the phone or counter.
Useful over noisy streets or bad phone lines.

exercises.prompt: Someone just said something too fast for you to catch. Tell them you didn't understand and ask them to repeat it.
A shopkeeper is talking quickly. Interrupt politely and ask them to slow down.
Someone tells you their name but you're not sure how it's spelled. Ask them to spell it out for you.
You hear a word you've never heard before in the middle of what someone's telling you. Interrupt them to ask what it means, without losing the thread of the conversation.

You're meeting someone new and you catch their name but not clearly enough to say it back confidently. Greet them, then handle it: ask them to repeat their name, and if you still can't catch it, ask them to spell it.

content.intro: You'll learn to understand and say prices in guaraníes, including the thousands where most everyday prices sit. The trap: Paraguayan prices are almost always in the thousands or millions, and locals routinely drop the word 'mil' in slang (diez luca = 10,000 Gs.), so a number said fast can go by before you convert it in your head — that's why this lesson leans on asking for a repeat.

vocab.note: cinco mil = 5,000; the base unit of nearly all everyday prices.
diez luca = 10,000 guaraníes; very common in spoken Paraguayan Spanish.
Interchangeable with ¿cuánto es? in shops and markets.
'son' (plural) agrees with amounts of money, not 'es'.

vocab.gloss: can you repeat the price for me?
vocab.note: Recycled from Lesson 2 — essential when a number goes by too fast.

exercises.prompt: You're at a kiosco. Ask the vendor how much a bottle of water costs.
The vendor answers with a price. Say the amount back to confirm you understood — for example, if they said fifteen thousand guaraníes.
The vendor mumbles the price and you only catch part of it. Ask them to repeat the price.
A friend tells you their phone cost 'dos palos' — say back in full guaraníes what that number is, then ask if you understood correctly.

You're buying several items at a small shop and the total comes out complicated — over a hundred thousand guaraníes. Ask the price, then confirm the total back to the shopkeeper, asking them to repeat it if you're not sure.

content.intro: You'll learn to order food from a street cart or bakery, ask for a quantity, and confirm the total price. The trap: quantities go before the item and often skip the article — 'dame dos empanadas' not 'dame las dos empanadas' — and prices here are always in guaraníes (Gs.), so keep last lesson's numbers ready.

vocab.gloss: traditional Paraguayan cheese bread, often made with cassava starch
vocab.note: Sold everywhere from street carts, especially mornings and bus terminals.
The most common variety, chewy texture.
A staple root vegetable, base of chipa and many dishes.
Usually filled with meat, chicken, or cheese.
Same use as ¿cuánto sale? from Lesson 3.
Quantity + item, no article — 'dame dos chipas' not 'dame las dos chipas'.
Chipa fresh out of the oven is often advertised as 'caliente'.
Prices are almost always written as 'Gs. 5.000'.

exercises.prompt: You walk up to a chipa cart. Ask the vendor how much the chipa costs.
Order three chipas from the vendor, and ask if they have any hot ones.
You want two empanadas to take away, not to eat there. Order them accordingly.
After ordering, ask for the total price, and if the vendor's answer goes by too fast, ask them to repeat it.

You're at a busy street stall with a short line behind you. Order a mix of chipa and empanadas in the quantities you want, ask if any are hot, confirm the total, and say it's to go — handle the whole exchange in one go.
